name: SPTAN1-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (alpha-II spectrin encephalopathy)

clinicalPearls: SPTAN1 encodes the non-erythrocytic alpha-II spectrin that forms the sub-membranous cytoskeletal scaffold of neurons and axons; in-frame dominant variants exert a dominant-negative effect on the spectrin heterodimer.
The severe classic phenotype presents in early infancy with an epileptic encephalopathy, frequently West syndrome with infantile spasms and hypsarrhythmia evolving to intractable seizures.
A highly suggestive imaging triad is progressive/acquired microcephaly, diffuse cerebral and brainstem atrophy, and widespread hypomyelination.
Affected infants typically show profound developmental delay or arrest, spastic quadriparesis and, in many, no purposeful hand use.
The clustering of in-frame deletions/duplications in the C-terminal region encoding the alpha/beta-spectrin nucleation site correlates with the most severe disease.
Milder or intermediate presentations exist, including generalised or focal epilepsy with less prominent atrophy and preserved head growth, particularly with certain missense or truncating variants.
Nystagmus, cortical visual impairment and dysphagia requiring feeding support are common in the severe form.
The disorder is genetically distinct from erythrocyte spectrin (SPTA1) disease and is not associated with haemolytic anaemia.
reference.pathophysiology: SPTAN1 encodes alpha-II spectrin (non-erythrocytic alpha-spectrin), a large cytoskeletal protein that pairs with beta-spectrin to build the flexible sub-plasma-membrane lattice that stabilises the neuronal membrane, organises the axon initial segment and nodes of Ranvier, and supports axonal transport and synaptic organisation. The severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy is characteristically caused by heterozygous in-frame deletions or duplications in the C-terminal domain that mediates alpha-beta spectrin heterodimer nucleation; the mutant protein still incorporates into the tetramer but disrupts its assembly, producing pathological aggregation of alpha-II and beta-II/III spectrins and a dominant-negative failure of the axonal cytoskeleton. This impairs myelination and axonal integrity, giving the radiological hallmark of hypomyelination with progressive cerebral, cerebellar and brainstem atrophy and acquired microcephaly. Variants that cause haploinsufficiency (truncating or missense) or that fall outside the nucleation region tend to produce milder phenotypes, so the position and type of variant are important determinants of severity.
additionalDifferentials: STXBP1, CDKL5, KCNQ2 and ARX developmental and epileptic encephalopathies presenting with infantile spasms
Other genetic causes of West syndrome and early-infantile epileptic encephalopathy
Pontocerebellar hypoplasias with progressive atrophy and microcephaly
Congenital disorders of glycosylation presenting with encephalopathy and atrophy
Perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (acquired mimic of atrophy and microcephaly)
Mitochondrial encephalopathies with regression and brainstem involvement
additionalInvestigations: Trio exome or genome sequencing with careful assessment of in-frame indels in the C-terminal domain (copy-number/breakpoint analysis may be needed)
Brain MRI to demonstrate hypomyelination, cerebral/brainstem atrophy and acquired microcephaly, with follow-up imaging to show progression
Electroencephalography looking for hypsarrhythmia or multifocal epileptiform activity
Ophthalmology and visual electrophysiology for cortical visual impairment and nystagmus
Swallow assessment and nutritional review for dysphagia
Deletion/duplication (CNV) analysis if sequencing is non-diagnostic but phenotype is characteristic
redFlags: Onset of infantile spasms or evolution to intractable seizures/status epilepticus
Progressive deceleration of head growth with developmental arrest or regression
Worsening bulbar function with aspiration risk
Rapid radiological progression of atrophy suggesting an alternative neurodegenerative process to reconsider
Acute clinical deterioration during intercurrent illness
reference.prognosis: The severe in-frame variant phenotype carries a poor prognosis with profound intellectual disability, spastic quadriparesis, drug-resistant epilepsy and shortened life expectancy, whereas milder variant classes can be associated with better developmental outcomes and more controllable epilepsy. Management is supportive and multidisciplinary.
pitfalls: Confusing SPTAN1 (neuronal alpha-II spectrin) with SPTA1 (erythrocyte alpha-spectrin); SPTAN1 disease does not cause hereditary spherocytosis or haemolysis.
Interpreting the hypomyelination and atrophy as a primary leukodystrophy and stopping the genetic work-up prematurely.
Missing pathogenic in-frame deletions/duplications because standard variant filtering can overlook small copy-number changes.
Assuming all SPTAN1 variants are severe; not every variant produces the classic devastating encephalopathy, so genotype should guide counselling.
Mistaking the picture for fixed perinatal brain injury and failing to recognise the progressive, acquired microcephaly.
